about: The one place in the Ordinary of the Mass that names the sacrifices of the Old Testament: Abel, Abraham and Melchisedech. The same three stand at one altar in the mosaic of Sant'Apollinare in Classe outside Ravenna. The prayer asks God to accept this sacrifice as He accepted theirs — and asks it after the consecration, which gave the medieval commentators trouble. Abel is here púer tuus iustus, Thy just servant. Melchisedech is summus sacérdos, Thy high priest. The rough seam of the closing words has a name in the tradition: the Liber Pontificalis says Leo the Great added sanctum sacrifícium, immaculátam hóstiam.

s01.narrative: The priest goes on with his hands spread.

s02.translation: Be pleased to look upon these offerings with a serene and kindly countenance, and to accept them, as once You were pleased to accept the gifts of Your servant Abel the just, and the sacrifice of Abraham, our father in faith:

s03.translation: and the offering of Your high priest Melchisedech, a holy sacrifice, a spotless victim.

w002.function: A relative with no antecedent clause, reaching back to the offerings of the prayer before. Latin opens a paragraph this way, English cannot.

w003.function: The first of the pair of epithets with “vultu” (w006): a word of Roman prayer for a god well-disposed to the asker — see the lemma.

w005.function: The second of the pair of epithets with “vultu” (w006): a face without a cloud — see the lemma for the word’s road from sky to countenance.

w011.function: Accépta habére — the idiom of the Te ígitur (there: accépta hábeas): to hold as received, to enter on the list of the accepted.

w015.function: A deponent participle with es: passive in form, active in meaning, and perfect in tense.

w016.function: The auxiliary: the tense is carried by the participle “dignátus” (w015), which is what the gloss renders.

w018.function: Puer means both boy and servant, as Greek país does.

w021.function: An indeclinable name: only “púeri” (w018), which it stands in apposition to, shows the genitive.

w026.function: The one of the three names Latin declines: Ábraham, Ábrahæ.

w028.function: A relative with no antecedent: that which he offered. Two appositions close the sentence after it.

w031.function: Paired with “sacérdos” (w032). In Gen 14 the epithet stands with God — sacérdos Dei altíssimi. The Canon moves it to the priest.

w034.function: Indeclinable: the nominative follows from its apposition to “sacérdos” (w032) — Melchisedech is the subject of “óbtulit” (w030). Alone of the three he offered what we offer, bread and wine.

w036.function: In apposition to “quod” (w028): the thing he offered — a holy sacrifice.

w038.function: The second of the two appositions to “quod” (w028). Feminine beside the neuter relative — apposition agrees in case alone.
